author: Stone Fox Capital
title: Fitbit: Med-Tech Future - Fitbit, Inc. (NYSE:FIT)
text:
A prime reason that Fitbit ( FIT ) was a solid gamble at $5 was the way the company invested in the future while maintaining a large cash balance. The investment thesis was that another hit product would change the way the market thought of the fitness tracker and the Versa smartwatch appears a game changer for now. The recent pullback from the Citron Research hype provides another opportunity for those that missed the boat.
Source: Fitbit presentation
More Than Health Devices Fitbit announced that the Versa shipped more than one million devices within about six weeks of launching the smartwatch on April 16. At an average selling price of about $200, the shipments are worth over $200 million due to accessories and the Fitbit pay version costing $230.
Annual sales were forecast at $1.5 billion, so the amount is significant. The key to the Versa appears the positioning in the price point far below the $350 price of the latest Apple ( AAPL ) Watch version.
The announcement of the success of the Versa hid the initial success of female health tracking. Fitbit has already seen 2.4 million users add the feature to their app with over 500,000 users adding two or more retrospective periods.
The company is on the path to turn what were fitness trackers into more of a med-tech device. The recent announcement of new health apps that will be available on both the Versa and Ionic smartwatches highlights the shift to more integral health monitoring than just counting steps.
The Dexcom app for glucose monitoring is scheduled for a 2H release providing important tracking for diabetes patients to better track their condition. As well, work with both UnitedHealth ( UNH ) and Humana ( HUM ) provide more access to programs that will reward and encourage users to purchase Fitbit devices.
Combined with the Twine Health scalable coaching platform bought earlier this year, Fitbit is positioned to move beyond just collecting steps via devices. The company is set up for monitoring health activities, collecting data for research efforts, and most importantly, improving health outcomes via timely data alerts and providing coaching/training along with rewards to make consumers healthier.
Source: Fitbit presentation
Financials Now that Fitbit has the ecosystem and devices in place, the market will want to see some improving financials. Lots of promise in the health and fitness segment won't matter if consumers don't actually buy and utilize the products.
As Citron Research pointed out with a $15 target on the stock, sales remain an issue but aggressive research and development spending has hidden the ability to generate positive cash flows. If the company so decided, Fitbit could generate more positive financials in the short term.
Fitbit is now spending nearly $90 million a quarter on R&D. The amount is roughly 25% of the $1.5 billion sales target.
FIT Research and Development Expense (Quarterly) data by YCharts
On a non-GAAP basis, the R&D spending was $75 million. Cutting the annual amount from $300 million to only $220 million or about 15% of sales would eliminate the forecast 2018 loss.
The company bought assets from Pebble and Coin amongst others that helped transition the devices into the smartwatch category and offer Fitbit Pay now. The balance sheet allows investors to stay confident while Fitbit remains in the investment phase. Spending aggressively on R&D is the only way to capture market share in the wearable sector and future health opportunities in med tech.
The company had $658 million in cash at the end of Q1 plus a combined $360 million in inventory and receivables. Fitbit even expects $80 million in tax refunds to boost the cash balance.
Source: Fitbit presentation
Calling Fitbit a medical device is probably stretching it, but a platform that provides access to health and fitness is just as valuable. The devices will likely handle multiple medical tracking capabilities as opposed to existing medical devices that focus on one particular health condition.
The reality is that Fitbit could have upside in excess of $15. The success of Versa and the expanding wearables market sets the company up for growth. Revenues growing to $2 billion based on market growth and a simple 3x sales multiple places the market cap around $6 billion. Not factoring in the cash balances, the share count of 240 million shares would generate a stock price nearly double the Citron target.
Note that Citron uses the 2018 revenue estimate of slightly below $1.5 billion and applies a 30% discount to the Garmin ( GRMN ) multiple. In essence, the near double from trading around $6.50 now is more of normalization of the valuation and not anything rewarding Fitbit of a med-tech device or tech platform related multiple.
Takeaway The key investor takeaway is that Fitbit now has the parts in place to realize the fitness and health platform benefits moving the stock and company away from the fad platform valuation. The company will continue losing money due to R&D spending that supports the move into med-tech applications that will eventually reward Fitbit with a higher valuation multiple.
